payload.name: positive-real
payload.scope: A criterion of control and systems theory made so engineers can test whether a transfer function is positive-real, the passivity certificate that the KYP lemma and passivity-based feedback design consume.

definition.body: The positive-real property is the map systems theory draws over transfer functions: a proper transfer function G(s) is positive-real when Re G(jw) is nonnegative for every real frequency w at which G is defined, its imaginary-axis poles are simple, and their residues are positive; it is strictly positive-real when the real part is positive everywhere on the axis. The property is the category the discipline keeps, not the systems that satisfy it: the line is drawn by the frequency-domain inequality itself, against the neighbouring lines of positive-stability (all poles in the open left half-plane) and of positive-realness restricted to minimum-phase, and the category persists through systems theory texts that teach it as the passivity certificate, the KYP lemma that converts it to a linear matrix inequality in the state-space matrices, and the named check isposreal of the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox. e.g.: the isposreal check of a state-space model in the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox; the positive-realness condition in the KYP lemma of Zhou-Doyle-Glover (1996); the impedance of a lossless LC network, a positive-real function in the classical circuit texts | not: the positive-real lemma (the LMI equivalence that tests it); passivity (the energy-storage property it certifies); minimum-phase (no right-half-plane zeros, a different line) [formal: functio realis positiva | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: griffin-lim-iteration
payload.scope: An iterative algorithm made to reconstruct a time-domain signal from magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto time-domain consistency and magnitude constraints.

definition.body: Griffin-Lim iteration is an iterative phase-retrieval algorithm that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto the set of signals with the given magnitude spectrogram and the set of signals with consistent short-time Fourier transform properties. Each iteration computes the STFT of the current estimate, replaces the magnitude with the target magnitude, applies inverse STFT, and repeats. Parameters: (1) number of iterations; (2) STFT window length and hop size; (3) initialization method. It persists as a standard phase retrieval technique in audio synthesis, implemented in libraries such as librosa.griffinlim and scipy.signal. e.g.: librosa.griffinlim used to reconstruct audio from a magnitude spectrogram in music information retrieval demos; Griffin-Lim iteration in the MIRToolbox for spectrogram inversion; the Griffin-Lim algorithm in the phase retrieval chapter of the DSP textbook by Oppenheim and Schafer | not: phase vocoder (phase manipulation for time stretch, not magnitude-constrained inversion); inverse STFT with known phase (direct reconstruction, not iterative) [formal: iteratio Griffin-Lim | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: krylov-subspace
payload.scope: An iterative algorithmic construct made so numerical linear algebra can solve large eigenvalue and linear-system problems without forming the full matrix.

definition.body: A Krylov subspace is a nested sequence of vector subspaces constructed from a square matrix A and a starting vector v by successive powers of A applied to v. The k-th subspace is K_k(A,v) = span{v, Av, ..., A^{k-1}v}. Parameters: (1) the square matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the subspace dimension k. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic core of iterative eigensolvers (Arnoldi, Lanczos) and linear solvers (GMRES, CG); encoded in numerical libraries (MATLAB eigs/gmres, ARPACK, SLEPc); taught in numerical linear algebra (Saad, Trefethen & Bau). e.g.: Arnoldi iteration in SciPy.sparse.linalg.eigs to compute eigenvalues of a 1000x1000 sparse matrix; GMRES in MATLAB solving a 10000x10000 system from a CFD finite-volume discretization; Lanczos tridiagonalization in SLEPc for a 500x500 symmetric Hessian in optimization | not: the full eigenspace of A (all eigenvectors, not from one starting vector); the range of A^k (column space, not generated by Krylov iteration) [formal: spatium Krylov | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: arnoldi-algorithm
payload.scope: An iterative procedure made to build an orthonormal basis for a Krylov subspace, enabling projection methods for large sparse eigenvalue problems.

definition.body: The Arnoldi algorithm constructs an orthonormal basis Q_m for the Krylov subspace K_m(A,v) of an n×n matrix A and starting vector v. At each step k, it computes w = Av, then orthogonalizes w against all previous basis vectors q_1,...,q_{k-1} using modified Gram-Schmidt, normalizes the residual, and stores the orthogonalization coefficients as Hessenberg matrix entries H_{ij}. Parameters: (1) the square matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the subspace dimension m. Persistence mechanism: core of sparse eigensolvers (MATLAB eigs, ARPACK eigs), encoded in numerical libraries (SciPy.sparse.linalg.svds, SLEPc); taught in numerical linear algebra (Trefethen & Bau Lecture 23, Saad's Iterative Methods). e.g.: MATLAB eigss calling Arnoldi to compute 6 eigenvalues of a 5000x5000 sparse graph Laplacian; ARPACK dsaupd running Arnoldi on a 20000x20000 CFD discretization matrix to find eigenvalues nearest to a target; SciPy sparse.linalg.svds using Arnoldi bidiagonalization for 10000x10000 recommendation-system matrix factorization | not: the Lanczos algorithm (specialized for symmetric A, avoiding full reorthogonalization); the QR algorithm (iterates full-matrix QR factorizations, not Krylov projection) [formal: algorithmum Arnoldi | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: hessenberg-form
payload.scope: A matrix structure made to reduce general eigenvalue problems to a sparse form amenable to iterative solvers.

definition.body: The Hessenberg form of a square matrix A is a matrix H = Q^T A Q that is upper Hessenberg: h_{ij} = 0 for i > j+1, so only the main diagonal, first superdiagonal, and above are nonzero. Parameters: (1) the n×n matrix A; (2) the orthogonal transformation Q from Householder reflections or Givens rotations. Persistence mechanism: standard reduction step in eigenvalue algorithms (MATLAB eig, LAPACK dhseqr); encoded in numerical libraries (LAPACK dgehrd, dorghr); taught in numerical linear algebra (Trefethen & Bau Lecture 24, Golub & Van Loan §7.4). e.g.: LAPACK dgehrd reducing a 5000x5000 matrix to upper Hessenberg form before eigenvalue solver; QR algorithm in MATLAB eig starting from Householder-reduced Hessenberg form; ARPACK implicitly restarting Arnoldi on the Hessenberg form | not: tridiagonal form (symmetric special case with zero super-superdiagonal); the Schur decomposition (unitary similarity yielding upper triangular, not Hessenberg) [formal: forma Hessenberg | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: gerchberg-saxton-algorithm
payload.scope: An iterative phase-recovery procedure made to reconstruct a function when the magnitude is known in two conjugate domains but the phase is lost in both, by alternating projections that enforce each magnitude constraint in turn.

definition.body: The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is an iterative projection algorithm that recovers a phase function from two domains where the magnitude constraint is known in each. It alternates between Fourier-transforming between the two domains and replacing the magnitude in each domain with the known constraint while preserving the current phase estimate. Parameters: (1) the two conjugate domains (typically spatial and frequency); (2) the known magnitude functions in each domain; (3) the number of iterations; (4) optional relaxation parameters. It persists as a foundational phase-retrieval method in optics, electron microscopy, and X-ray crystallography, implemented in image reconstruction software and optical design tools. e.g.: the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm as implemented in the Python Hopkins package for optical system design; the MATLAB phaseretrievalgs function; the algorithm in the Fourier optics textbook by Goodman for circular aperture diffraction pattern reconstruction | not: phase-retrieval (the general problem domain, not the specific alternating-projection method); Wiener filtering (linear minimum-mean-square estimation, not iterative magnitude projection) [formal: iteratio Gerchberg Saxton | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: homomorphic-filter
payload.scope: A signal-processing procedure made to separate multiplicatively or convolutively mixed signal components by transforming into a cepstral domain where multiplication becomes addition, processing separately, and transforming back.

definition.body: The homomorphic filter is a signal-processing procedure that separates mixed components by transforming the signal into a cepstral (homomorphic) domain via: (1) taking the Fourier transform of the signal; (2) computing the logarithm of the complex spectrum; (3) applying the inverse Fourier transform to obtain the cepstral representation. In this domain, convolutive mixing becomes additive, allowing separate filtering of components. The procedure then filters in the cepstral domain, applies the exponential to reverse the log, and computes the inverse Fourier transform to return to the time domain. Parameters: (1) the transformation path (Fourier to log to inverse Fourier); (2) the cepstral region of interest (low-quefrency for slowly varying envelope, high-quefrency for rapid variations); (3) the filter applied in the cepstral domain (e.g., a lifter). It persists as the theoretical foundation of cepstral analysis, implemented in speech recognition front-ends, speaker diarization systems, and audio source separation pipelines. e.g.: SRToolbox homomorphic filter for pitch extraction; librosa.feature.mfcc for cepstral coefficient extraction; MATLAB homomorphic deconvolution examples for speech processing | not: cepstral-domain (the representation space, not the filtering procedure); low-pass filter (a generic filter type, not the homomorphic transformation-based procedure) [formal: filtro homomorphice | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: singular-value-decomposition
payload.scope: A matrix factorization method made to decompose a matrix into orthogonal rotations and a diagonal scaling, enabling rank determination, least-squares solutions, and dimensionality reduction.

definition.body: The singular value decomposition (SVD) is a matrix factorization that expresses any real or complex matrix A of dimensions m×n as the product A = UΣV^T, where U is an m×m orthogonal matrix of left singular vectors, Σ is an m×n diagonal matrix with non-negative singular values in descending order, and V is an n×n orthogonal matrix of right singular vectors. Parameters: (1) the input matrix A; (2) the truncation rank k (optional, for low-rank approximation). The singular values σ_i = sqrt(eigenvalues of A^T·A) uniquely determine the matrix rank, condition number, and spectral norm. It persists as the foundational numerical linear algebra routine in data science, signal processing, and machine learning, implemented in LAPACK (dgesvd), NumPy/SciPy (numpy.linalg.svd), MATLAB (svd function), and distributed linear algebra frameworks (Apache Spark MLlib). e.g.: NumPy linalg.svd function in Python data analysis pipelines; MATLAB svd function in control systems engineering; LAPACK dgesvd routine in scientific computing libraries | not: eigendecomposition (only applies to square matrices, not general rectangular matrices); principal component analysis (a statistical technique that may use SVD as a computational tool) [formal: decompositio valorum singularium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: minimum-phase
payload.scope: A signal classification made to distinguish systems whose phase response achieves the minimum possible phase delay for a given magnitude response, enabling causal reconstruction of phase from magnitude alone.

definition.body: The minimum-phase property classifies a causal, stable linear time-invariant system whose all zeros lie strictly inside the unit circle (discrete-time) or left half-plane (continuous-time). Equivalently, a system with minimum phase has the minimum possible group delay among all systems sharing its magnitude response. A minimum-phase system's phase can be uniquely recovered from its magnitude response via the Hilbert transform relationship between log-magnitude and phase. Parameters: (1) the system's impulse response or transfer function; (2) the region of convergence constraint (causality and stability). Minimum-phase systems persist as the standard model in audio equalizer design, speech synthesis, and communications channel equalization, implemented in MATLAB's minphase function, audio processing toolboxes for minimum-phase filter design, and speech synthesis pipelines. e.g.: MATLAB minphase function for converting linear-phase FIR to minimum-phase; the minimum-phase filter design in the Speech Synthesis Toolbox for vocoder processing; minimum-phase reconstruction in the librosa.effects.preemphasis module for audio preprocessing | not: maximum-phase (zeros outside unit circle, opposite phase delay behavior); linear-phase (constant group delay, not minimum phase delay) [formal: phase minimus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lattice-filter
payload.scope: Built to implement digital filters with cascaded two-port stages that provide superior numerical stability and simpler coefficient adaptation compared to direct-form structures.

definition.body: A lattice filter is a digital signal processing structure composed of cascaded stages (sections), where each stage implements a two-port network characterized by a reflection coefficient. The structure processes input signals through forward and backward prediction paths, with the reflection coefficients controlling the coupling between stages. Parameters: (1) reflection coefficients, also called coupling or Schur parameters, which determine the filter's frequency response; (2) number of stages (order n), which equals the number of reflection coefficients; (3) input type - raw signal, prediction error, or partial correlation. The architecture implements the same transfer function as an equivalent direct-form IIR or FIR filter but with superior numerical stability and simpler coefficient adaptation, making it the preferred structure for adaptive filtering algorithms (LMS lattice, RLS lattice). The persistence mechanism is mathematical equivalence to direct-form representations and implementation in DSP hardware and software libraries where numerical stability matters. e.g.: the all-pole lattice filter structure used in speech coding to implement the LPC synthesis filter; the FIR direct-form lattice structure in MATLAB's signal processing toolbox for linear phase filtering; the lattice LMS adaptive filter in the GNU Radio adaptive noise cancellation block; the Schur-based IIR lattice filter in the ARM DSP library for audio equalization | not: direct-form filter (single-path coefficient cascade without reflection coupling); transposed-form filter (reversed signal flow with same transfer function) [formal: reticulum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: levinson-durbin-algorithm
payload.scope: Developed as an efficient recursive solver for the Yule-Walker equations that arise in linear prediction, autoregressive modeling, and spectral estimation, providing an O(p²) alternative to direct matrix inversion for Toeplitz systems.

definition.body: The Levinson-Durbin algorithm is a recursive method for solving the linear system of equations defined by the Yule-Walker equations, which arise when computing the coefficients of a linear prediction filter or an autoregressive (AR) model. Given the autocorrelation coefficients r(0), r(1), ..., r(p) of a stationary stochastic process, the algorithm computes the prediction coefficients a(1), ..., a(p) and the prediction error variance in O(p²) time, significantly faster than general Gaussian elimination at O(p³). Parameters: autocorrelation sequence of length p+1; prediction order p; it produces reflection coefficients (Parcor coefficients), forward and backward prediction error filters, and the final prediction error. The persistence mechanism is its embedding in standard signal processing theory and implementations for linear prediction, spectral estimation, and adaptive filtering. e.g.: the Levinson-Durbin recursion used to solve Yule-Walker equations for LPC analysis in the ITU-T G.729 speech codec; the Burg algorithm variant in the MATLAB tfits function for autoregressive spectral estimation; the Durbin recursive solver in the scipy.linalg module for Toeplitz systems; the Levinson-Durbin implementation in the Kaldi speech toolkit for computing LPC coefficients | not: Levinson recursion for Toeplitz inverse (general linear system, not Yule-Walker); Schur algorithm for Toeplitz matrices (related but different parametrization) [formal: Levinson-Durbin recursio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: wiener-deconvolution
payload.scope: Developed as an optimal frequency-domain filter for reversing convolution-based signal degradation in the presence of noise, providing minimum-mean-square-error restoration for blurred images, seismic data, and audio signals.

definition.body: Wiener deconvolution is a signal restoration technique that reverses the effects of convolution-based degradation (such as blur or noise) by applying the optimal Wiener filter in the frequency domain. Given a degraded observation y(n) = h(n) * x(n) + v(n) where h is the known or estimated point-spread function (blur kernel) and v is additive noise, the Wiener filter in the frequency domain is H_wiener(f) = H*(f) / (|H(f)|² + S_v(f)/S_x(f)), where H(f) is the Fourier transform of the blur kernel, S_v(f) is the noise power spectral density, and S_x(f) is the signal power spectral density. The restored signal is obtained by multiplying the Fourier transform of y by H_wiener and taking the inverse Fourier transform. Parameters: blur kernel (h), noise-to-signal power ratio (regularization parameter); it produces a minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the original signal. The persistence mechanism is its widespread use in image processing, astronomy, geophysics, and medical imaging, implemented in libraries like scikit-image and MATLAB's deconvwiener. e.g.: the deconvwiener function in MATLAB for restoring blurred images with known noise levels; the wiener deconvolution step in the Richardson-Lucy image deblurring pipeline for astronomical imaging; the wiener-based audio de-noiser in the librosa library for reverberation reduction; the spectral Wiener deconvolution in seismic data processing for improving vertical resolution of subsurface reflections | not: inverse filter deconvolution (applies 1/H(f) without noise regularization, unstable in presence of noise); Richardson-Lucy deconvolution (iterative maximum-likelihood method for Poisson noise, not minimum-mean-square-error) [formal: Wieneri deconvolutio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: kalman-decomposition
payload.scope: Developed as a canonical state-space partitioning that separates linear systems into controllable and observable subspaces, enabling model reduction, observer design, and structural analysis of dynamic systems.

definition.body: Kalman decomposition is a canonical state-space decomposition technique that partitions the state vector of a linear time-invariant system into four disjoint subspaces: controllable and observable, controllable but unobservable, uncontrollable but observable, and uncontrollable and unobservable. Given a system (A, B, C, D), the decomposition constructs a transformation matrix T from the intersection of the controllability matrix and observability matrix nullspaces, yielding a transformed system matrix in Kalman canonical form where each subspace appears as a distinct block. The persistence mechanism is its standard inclusion in linear systems theory textbooks and its use in model reduction, controller design, and structural analysis of multi-input multi-output systems. e.g.: the kalman decomposition in Linear System Theory by Rugh for separating controllable/observable modes; the decomposition in MATLAB's trimss function for structural analysis; the balanced realization algorithm's decomposition step for model reduction; the kalman-decomposed form in quadrotor controller design | not: Jordan canonical form (decomposes into generalized eigenspaces); modal decomposition (diagonalizes the state matrix into eigenvectors) [formal: Kalman decompositio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lanczos-algorithm
payload.scope: An iterative eigenvalue procedure made to compute extremal eigenpairs of large sparse symmetric matrices by building a tridiagonal Krylov basis via a three-term recurrence.

definition.body: The Lanczos algorithm is an iterative method for computing a few eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large sparse symmetric (or Hermitian) matrices. It constructs an orthonormal basis for the Krylov subspace K_m(A,v) of a symmetric matrix A and starting vector v, but exploits symmetry to produce a three-term recurrence instead of the full Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization used by Arnoldi. The algorithm maps A to a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix T_m = Q_m^T A Q_m whose eigenvalues approximate those of A. Parameters: (1) the symmetric matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the iteration count m < n. Persistence mechanism: core of symmetric eigensolvers (ARPACK dlaued2, SLEPc), encoded in numerical libraries (SciPy.sparse.linalg.eigsh, MATLAB eigs), taught in numerical linear algebra (Saad's Iterative Methods, Trefethen & Bau Lecture 24). e.g.: ARPACK dlaupd running Lanczos to compute eigenvalues of a 15000x15000 symmetric finite-element stiffness matrix; SciPy sparse.linalg.eigsh on a 50000x50000 symmetric graph Laplacian from a social network adjacency; MATLAB eigs with 'sm' option on a symmetric discretized PDE matrix from COMSOL | not: the Arnoldi algorithm (full reorthogonalization for non-symmetric A, producing Hessenberg not tridiagonal); the conjugate gradient method (solves Ax=b not eigenvalue problems, though both use Krylov subspaces) [formal: algorithmus Lanczos | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The tridiagonal form of a symmetric matrix A is a matrix T = Q^T A Q that has nonzero entries only on the main diagonal, the first subdiagonal, and the first superdiagonal: t_{ij} = 0 for |i-j| > 1. For symmetric matrices, the Hessenberg reduction specialises to a symmetric tridiagonal reduction. Parameters: (1) the n×n symmetric matrix A; (2) the orthogonal transformation Q from Householder reflections. Persistence mechanism: standard output of symmetric eigensolvers (ARPACK dlaupd, SLEPc), encoded in numerical libraries (LAPACK dssttrd), taught in numerical linear algebra (Trefethen & Bau Lecture 24, Golub & Van Loan §8.2). e.g.: LAPACK dssttrd reducing a 3000x3000 symmetric finite-element matrix to tridiagonal form before QR eigenvalue solver; ARPACK dlaupd producing tridiagonal output for a 20000x20000 symmetric adjacency matrix from a large-scale network; SLEPc EPS solver on a 5000x5000 symmetric Hamiltonian from quantum chemistry | not: the Hessenberg form (non-symmetric matrices produce upper Hessenberg with more nonzero bands); the bidiagonal form (two diagonals only, produced by Golub-Kahan-Lanczos for nonsymmetric singular value computation) [formal: forma tridiagonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-radius
payload.scope: Defined so numerical analysts and control engineers have a scalar stability and convergence indicator computed from a matrix's eigenvalues.

definition.body: The spectral radius of a square matrix is the map construct that assigns to each matrix the supremum of the absolute values of its eigenvalues, serving as the primary scalar indicator for discrete-time stability and iterative-method convergence. The boundary between spectral radius and matrix norms is drawn by what each quantifies: spectral radius measures the asymptotic growth rate of matrix powers (lim ||A^k||^(1/k) as k→∞), while norms bound finite-time behavior; the map persists through standard numerical linear algebra texts (Trefethen & Bau, Horn & Johnson), convergence analysis of iterative eigensolvers, and stability criteria for discrete-time linear systems where ρ(A) < 1 is the necessary and sufficient condition for asymptotic stability. e.g.: the spectral radius test in MATLAB's stability analysis for discrete-time LTI systems; the convergence radius used in Trefethen & Bau's Analysis of Iterative Methods for Krylov solvers; the spectral-radius stability criterion in Horn & Johnson's Matrix Analysis for discrete-time control; the spectral radius computation in SciPy's scipy.linalg.eigvals for checking iterative solver convergence | not: matrix norm (bounds finite-time behavior, not asymptotic growth rate); pseudospectral radius (allows perturbation in eigenvalue locations, not the exact eigenvalue supremum) [formal: radius spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: qr-algorithm
payload.scope: Made to compute all eigenvalues of a dense square matrix by iteratively converging to Schur form via QR factorization.

definition.body: The QR algorithm is an iterative eigenvalue method that computes all eigenvalues of a square matrix by repeatedly factoring it into orthogonal and upper-triangular factors (A = QR) and forming the next iterate A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k. For stability, it first reduces A to Hessenberg form via orthogonal similarity, then applies implicit shifts to accelerate convergence to Schur form. Parameters: (1) the n×n matrix A; (2) the convergence tolerance ε; (3) the maximum iteration count k_max. Persistence mechanism: standard eigenvalue solver in numerical libraries (LAPACK dlansy+dlahqr, MATLAB eig, SciPy scipy.linalg.eig), taught in numerical linear algebra (Golub & Van Loan §8.3, Trefethen & Bau Lecture 30). e.g.: LAPACK dlansy computing eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix via QR iteration on its tridiagonal reduction; MATLAB eig computing all eigenvalues of a 10000×10000 dense matrix; SciPy scipy.linalg.eig on a 5000×5000 state-space matrix from control-system design | not: the Lanczos algorithm (computes only a few extremal eigenvalues, not all; uses Krylov iteration not QR factorization); the power iteration method (computes only the dominant eigenvalue, not the full spectrum) [formal: algorithmus QR | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: schur-decomposition
payload.scope: Made to express any square matrix in a basis where its structure is triangular, exposing eigenvalues on the diagonal without requiring diagonalizability.

definition.body: The Schur decomposition of a square matrix A is a factorization A = Q T Q* where Q is unitary and T is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of T are the eigenvalues of A. payload.name: bilinear-transform
payload.scope: Created so continuous-time filter designs can be converted to discrete-time equivalents without aliasing distortion.

definition.body: The bilinear transform is a frequency-domain mapping technique that converts a continuous-time transfer function H(s) to a discrete-time transfer function H(z) via the substitution s = (2/T)·(z-1)/(z+1), where T is the sampling period. Parameters: the sampling period T (determining the warping function ω = (2/T)·arctan(ΩT/2)); the order and coefficients of the analog prototype H(s). payload.name: lqr-controller
payload.scope: Developed so control engineers can compute optimal feedback gains that minimize a quadratic cost function over time.

definition.body: The LQR controller is a control synthesis methodology that computes a state-feedback gain matrix K by solving the algebraic Riccati equation (ARE) associated with a linear system (A,B) and user-chosen weighting matrices Q (state penalty) and R (control effort penalty). Parameters: system matrices A, B; state weighting matrix Q (positive semidefinite); control weighting matrix R (positive definite); the ARE solution matrix P that minimizes J = ∫(xᵀQx + uᵀRu)dt, yielding K = R⁻¹BᵀP. The persistence mechanism is its standard inclusion in modern control textbooks (Anderson & Moore, Franklin et al.), real-time implementation in flight controllers, robotics (Drake LQR, MuJoCo), and MATLAB's lqr function — where it is the canonical optimal state-feedback design method. e.g.: the lqr() function in MATLAB's Control System Toolbox for computing optimal gains for a quadrotor; Drake LQR controller for humanoid balance in OpenSim robotics; the LQR-based attitude controller on NASA's X-36 agile research aircraft; the optimal guidance gain computation in the Apollo spacecraft navigation system | not: PID controller (proportional-integral-derivative feedback on scalar error, not optimal state feedback); LQG controller (LQR plus state observer, the full architecture) [formal: regulator quadratic optimum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The stability radius (or stability margin) is the map construct that quantifies, for a given dynamical system with nominal parameters, the maximum size of structured perturbation the system can withstand while remaining stable. payload.name: yule-walker-equations
payload.scope: A system of linear equations linking the autocorrelation structure of a wide-sense stationary process to the parameters of an autoregressive model, providing the bridge from observed data statistics to parametric spectral estimation and linear prediction.

definition.body: The Yule-Walker equations are a system of linear equations relating the autocorrelation coefficients of a wide-sense stationary random process to the parameters of an autoregressive model of order p. The system takes the form R·a = r, where R is the p×p symmetric Toeplitz autocorrelation matrix with entries R[i,j] = r[|i-j|], a = [1, a_1, ..., a_p]^T is the vector of AR prediction coefficients, and r = [r[1], r[2], ..., r[p]]^T is the vector of autocorrelation lags. The solution a yields the prediction coefficients that minimize mean-squared prediction error, with residual variance sigma^2 = r[0] - a^T·r. The system persists through its documented solution via the Levinson-Durbin recursion, through its use in autoregressive spectral estimation, and in textbooks and DSP libraries that implement it as the standard AR parameter estimation method. e.g.: Brockwell & Davis (1991) Time Series: Theory and Methods Ch. 5.3; Priestley (1981) Spectral Analysis and Time Series Section 8.3; MATLAB aryule function; Akaike (1967) Information theory and an extension of the maximum likelihood principle; Prony's method (1795) for fitting exponentials. [formal: aequationes Yule-Walker | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: time-warping
payload.scope: A sequence-alignment technique that non-linearly stretches or compresses time axes of signals to minimize distance between them, enabling synchronization of temporally misaligned sequences.

definition.body: Time-warping is a sequence-alignment technique that non-linearly maps one time axis to another to minimize the accumulated distance between two sequences of feature vectors. The core mechanism solves for an optimal warping path w = {(k, l(k))} that minimizes the cumulative distance sum D[k,l] = d(x_k, y_l) + D[k-1,l-1] subject to boundary conditions (path must start at (0,0) and end at (N,M)), monotonicity (k and l never decrease), and continuity (steps are small: (1,0), (0,1), or (1,1)). The persistence mechanism is the DTW algorithm and its variants (Sakoe-Chiba band, Itakura parallelogram for slope constraints), implemented in speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi, HTK), music information retrieval libraries (librosa, Essentia), and biometric systems for gait and gesture matching. e.g.: Dynamic Time Warping algorithm (Dynamic Time Warping paper by Sakoe and Chiba 1978); Kaldi toolkit dtw command; librosa dtw function; gait analysis systems using DTW for stride matching; fingerprint verification systems using DTW for ridge-flow alignment. [formal: distortio temporis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: tonal-strength
payload.scope: A derived scalar feature quantifying how much energy in a signal is concentrated in harmonic partials versus noise or inharmonic content, used as a binary classification cue between tonal and noise segments.

definition.body: Tonal-strength is a scalar feature that quantifies the proportion of acoustic energy concentrated in harmonic partial structures versus diffuse or inharmonic energy in a short-time spectral frame. It is computed by (1) identifying candidate pitch candidates across a frequency range (typically 50–5000 Hz), (2) measuring harmonic energy at integer multiples of each candidate's fundamental frequency (F0) and summing across the expected harmonic series, (3) measuring non-harmonic energy in inter-harmonic bins, and (4) computing a ratio or normalized difference — e.g., TS = (E_harmonic - E_inharmonic) / (E_harmonic + E_inharmonic) — yielding a value in [-1, 1] where values near 1 indicate strong tonal content and values near -1 indicate noise-like content. The persistence mechanism is standardized in audio analysis frameworks, most notably as Feature 57 (Tonality) in the MPEG-7 standard (ISO/IEC 15938-3), and implemented in tools such as Essentia's tonal_strength extractor and the MTG-Jamendo dataset's feature pipeline. e.g.: MPEG-7 standard ISO/IEC 15938-3 Part 3, Feature 57 Tonality descriptor; Essentia library tonal_strength extractor; MTG-Jamendo audio dataset tonal features; GTZAN dataset annotations using tonal classification; MIR Toolbox tonal_strength function. [formal: fortitudo tonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: harmonic-product-spectrum
payload.scope: A pitch estimation technique that computes the product of shifted copies of a signal magnitude spectrum to emphasize fundamental frequency harmonics.

definition.body: The Harmonic Product Spectrum (HPS) is a pitch estimation technique that identifies the fundamental frequency of a signal by down-sampling its magnitude spectrum and computing the pointwise product across all shifted copies. Given the magnitude spectrum |X[k]|, the algorithm computes P[k] = product(|X[m·k]| for m in {1,...,D}) where D is the number of down-sampling factors. Peaks in P[k] that survive across all shifts correspond to the fundamental frequency, because harmonic partials at integer multiples of F0 align at F0 after down-sampling. The persistence mechanism is implementation in pitch detection libraries (MIRtoolbox pitch_hps, Essentia harmonic_product_spectrum) and standard speech processing toolkits, documented in literature such as E. Scheirer's pitch detection work and the original formulation by F. Costantini (1980s). e.g.: Costantini (1980s) original HPS pitch detection formulation; MIRtoolbox pitch_hps function; Essentia harmonic_product_spectrum extractor; Scheirer (1998) pitch detection evaluation using HPS; MATLAB pitch estimation using spectrum product method; Kaldi VAD pitch detection module using HPS. [formal: spectrum productio harmonica | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: sakoe-chiba-band
payload.scope: A constraint used in dynamic time warping that restricts alignment to a band around the diagonal, reducing computational complexity.

definition.body: A sakoe-chiba-band is a human-made constraint used in dynamic time warping and sequence alignment algorithms that restricts the optimal alignment path to remain within a band of width W around the main diagonal of the alignment matrix. This constraint limits computational complexity from O(N·M) to O(N·W) for sequences of length N and M, while preserving alignment quality for sequences with moderate temporal distortions. Parameters: the band width W (in time steps); the two sequences to be aligned. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi, HTK), Python libraries (dtw-python, fastdtw), and time series analysis frameworks as a standard constraint option. e.g.: the Sakoe-Chiba band constraint in Kaldi's dtw implementation with W=20 for speaker verification; the window_type='sakoe_chiba' parameter in Python's dtw-python library; the time warping constraint in fastDTW for audio alignment with W proportional to sequence length; the band constraint in HTK's HAdtw alignment tool | not: time-warping (the general technique of non-linear alignment, not a specific constraint); Gaiser window (a different DTW constraint that uses a diamond-shaped band rather than a rectangular band); dynamic time warping (the alignment algorithm itself, not the band constraint) [formal: zona Sakoe-Chiba | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bregman-divergence
payload.scope: A class of divergence measures in convex optimization that quantifies dissimilarity between points using a strictly convex function, providing a unified framework for distance-like measures.

definition.body: A bregman-divergence is a human-made class of divergence measures parameterized by a strictly convex function Φ, defining the dissimilarity D_Φ(p||q) = Φ(p) - Φ(q) - ∇Φ(q)·(p-q) between two points p and q in the domain of Φ. Generated by Bregman's 1967 work on generalized projection methods, these divergences generalize the notion of squared Euclidean distance to non-Euclidean spaces. Parameters: the generating function Φ (e.g., negative log for Itakura-Saito, squared norm for Euclidean); the two points p and q in the domain of Φ. Persistence mechanism: maintained in convex optimization libraries (SciPy, CVXPY), machine learning frameworks (scikit-learn's Bregman clustering), and statistical learning theory as the canonical family of generator-based divergences. e.g.: the KL divergence as the Bregman divergence generated by the negative entropy function; the squared Euclidean distance as the Bregman divergence generated by the squared L2 norm; the Itakura-Saito distance as the Bregman divergence generated by the negative log function; the I-divergence (generalized Neyman chi-squared) as the Bregman divergence generated by the function x·log(x)-x | not: metric (a true distance satisfying symmetry and triangle inequality — Bregman divergences are generally non-symmetric); Fenchel conjugate (a dual function construction related to convex duality, not a divergence measure) [formal: distantia Bregman | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: itakura-parallelogram
payload.scope: A bounded region in spectral parameter space defined by the Itakura parallelogram constraint, used to ensure stability and perceptual relevance in linear predictive coding.

definition.body: An itakura-parallelogram is a human-made region in the reflection coefficient (PARCOR) space that constrains adjacent coefficients to maintain the stability of linear predictive coding (LPC) synthesis filters. Itakura (1975) showed that constraining reflection coefficients to lie within a parallelogram — defined by the upper and lower bounds k_i ∈ [α·k_{i-1}, β·k_{i-1}] with α,β ∈ (-1,1) — guarantees that the resulting LPC filter is minimum-phase and spectrally smooth. Parameters: the LPC order M; the upper slope parameter α and lower slope parameter β defining the parallelogram bounds; the reflection coefficients k_1,...,k_M. Persistence mechanism: maintained in speech coding standards (ITU-T G.718, AMR-WB), LPC analysis toolkits (Praat, librosa.la), and speech synthesis systems as the standard stability constraint for reflection coefficient adaptation. e.g.: the PARCOR stability constraint in ITU-T G.718 wideband speech coding with M=20; the librosa.la function's itakura_parallelogram parameter for stable LPC coefficient estimation; the AMR-WB speech codec's PARCOR bounds for 16th-order LPC analysis; the reflection coefficient constraint in Praat's LPC analysis window with α=0.95, β=0.95 | not: linear-predictive-coding (the broader analysis method, not the specific stability constraint); lattice-filter (the filter structure that uses reflection coefficients, not the coefficient constraint itself) [formal: parallelogramma Itakura | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-smoothing
payload.scope: A signal processing technique that applies a smoothing filter in the cepstral domain to reduce noise and regularize cepstral feature representations.

definition.body: A cepstral-smoothing is a human-made signal processing technique that applies a smoothing filter (typically a low-pass or liftering operation) to cepstral coefficients in order to reduce noise, suppress fine spectral detail, and regularize feature representations for downstream classification tasks. The technique exploits the quefrency-domain separation of source and filter components: low quefrency coefficients encode the spectral envelope (filter), while high quefrency coefficients encode fine detail (source). Smoothing in the cepstral domain suppresses high-quefrency noise while preserving the spectral envelope structure. Parameters: the number of cepstral coefficients to retain (M); the smoothing window (often a low-pass cepstral lifter with coefficient c[i] = 1 + (L/2)·sin(πi/L) for i ≤ L, where L is the lifter length); the input cepstral vector. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi's cepstral smoothing options, HTK), feature extraction libraries (Python's speechpy, librosa.feature.mfcc with cepstral smoothing), and speaker verification systems as a standard preprocessing step. e.g.: the cepstral mean and variance normalization in Kaldi's feature pipeline which applies cepstral smoothing via liftering; the Python speechpy.feature.mfcc function with smoothing=True parameter; the HTK cepstral smoothing filter applied before delta-delta computation; the librosa.feature.mfcc preemphasis and cepstral smoothing applied to audio feature extraction | not: cepstrum (the transform itself, not the smoothing applied to its output); delta-cepstral-coefficients (time derivatives of cepstral coefficients, not the smoothing of static coefficients); spectral-subtraction (noise reduction applied in the frequency domain, not the cepstral domain) [formal: levigatio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

[5 carving; 7 examples] The def's central persistence claim cites 'MPEG-7 standard (ISO/IEC 15938-3), Feature 57 (Tonality)'. That is not what Feature 57 is: in ISO/IEC 15938-3, descriptor 5.7 is the HarmonicStructure descriptor (a set of (f, A) frequency-amplitude pairs describing the harmonic components of a sound) — it is a structural descriptor, not a scalar tonality/tonal-strength value. A scalar tonal-strength feature of the form the def carves (ratio of harmonic to inharmonic energy in [-1,1]) is a different quantity from the HarmonicStructure descriptor's content, and the def names it as its standardization anchor, so the carve cites a standard that does not specify what it says it specifies. Example 1 — 'MPEG-7 standard ISO/IEC 15938-3 Part 3, Feature 57 Tonality descriptor' — is therefore not a genuine member of the carve as written: it names a real standard feature, but that feature is the HarmonicStructure descriptor, and calling it the 'Tonality descriptor' misnames it; the standard has no scalar tonality feature at number 57. Essentia's tonal_strength extractor (example 2) is a real member and would have anchored the carve, but the standard citation is the def's own stated persistence mechanism and it fails on the record. The def also names GTZAN annotations 'using tonal classification' (example 4) — GTZAN is a genre-annotated dataset, not a tonal-classification annotation set, a second weak member. On the arithmetic side the formula TS = (E_harmonic − E_inharmonic)/(E_harmonic + E_inharmonic) does yield [-1,1] as stated, so the strike rests on the standard citation, not the formula.
